title: Buffett Partnership letters 1965-67: beating the Dow, concentration, and conservatism
summary: Buffett's partnership letters from 1965-67 explain why he measures against the Dow, concentrates up to 40% in his best ideas, defines conservatism by facts and reasoning rather than convention, and values controlled businesses on assets and earning power. They also cover compounding, ignoring market forecasts, taxes, and the limits of size.

principles.text: Conservatism comes from correct facts and sound reasoning, not from doing what is conventional.
principles.quote: Truly conservative actions arise from intelligent hypotheses, correct facts and sound reasoning.

principles.text: Don't take comfort or discomfort from crowd agreement; understand the situation yourself.
principles.quote: A public opinion poll is no substitute for thought.

principles.text: Concentrate heavily in the best few ideas rather than owning dozens; over-diversification lowers expected results.
principles.quote: any portfolio encompassing one hundred stocks (whether the manager is handling one thousand dollars or one billion dollars) is not being operated logically.

principles.text: Accept bumpy short-term results for better long-term performance, but never risk permanent capital loss.
principles.quote: I am not willing to incur risk of substantial permanent capital loss in seeking to better long term performance.

principles.text: Focus on what a business will do, not when the market will recognize it; don't forecast the market.
principles.quote: we tend to concentrate on what should happen, not when it should happen.

principles.text: Maximize after-tax compounding by owning the best securities, not by minimizing taxes; don't confuse means with ends.
principles.quote: Means and end should not be confused, however, and the end is to come away with the largest after-tax rate of compound.
